articles.title: Matthew McConaughey started an after-school programme for underserved teens; it now serves more than 3,000 students across US cities
articles.summary: Just Keep Livin Foundation was founded by Camila and Matthew McConaughey to support high school students through after-school programmes.
articles.body: Just Keep Livin Foundation was founded by Camila and Matthew McConaughey to support high school students through after-school programmes. According to its 2022 Impact Report, the non-profit served over 3,000 students through 43 programmes across 15 cities in 2022. The programmes operate in Title 1 schools and cover nutrition, fitness, wellness and community service. The report states that students performed more than 7,200 hours of community service during 2022. It also records the foundation's work after the Uvalde shooting in May 2022, including a programme at Uvalde High School, a relief fund and a scholarship.How did McConaughey start the programmeThe foundation was founded by Camila and Matthew McConaughey with the mission of empowering high school students by giving them the tools to lead active lives and make healthy choices for a better future. The report describes the organisation as a non-profit that implements after-school fitness programmes in inner-city high schools. It states that participating students have a safe place to work with fitness coaches and health experts.The report names four pillars: nutrition, fitness, community service and wellness. The foundation operates in Title 1 schools, which have a large concentration of at-risk and low-income students. The report also states that more than 22,000 young people have been served since its inception.How does the programme promote healthy eatingThe nutrition component covers recipes for preparing healthy meals on a budget, outings to restaurants and farmers' markets, cooking demonstrations with chefs, nutritionists and food banks, and healthy snacks and water at each meeting. The report states that 94% of students make healthier eating choices. For fitness, it lists learning to use weights and exercise equipment, setting safe and realistic goals, group sports and guided workouts such as yoga and Zumba. The report says 95% of students in the programme get more exercise, and it notes that 70% of high school students do not meet the recommended daily amount of physical activity.The report describes the wellness component as a gratitude circle, guest speakers, journals and peer connection, and states that 90% of students feel increased gratitude. In the community service component, the report lists beautifying schools with City Year, cleaning beaches with Heal The Bay, packing troop care packages with Operation Gratitude and packing holiday food boxes with regional food banks. According to the report, students performed more than 7,200 hours of service, and 94% showed increased participation in community service. Its curriculum sample for November sets out a four-week plan: a goal-setting lesson, a guest speaker, a nutrition tip and a closing reflection.How many cities does it reachThe foundation reached 43 communities in 15 cities in 2022. It lists these as Los Angeles, San Diego, Austin, Dallas-Fort Worth, Uvalde, Longview and Houston in Texas and California, together with New Orleans, Nashville, Dublin in Georgia, Cleveland, Charlotte, Washington, D.C., New York and Chicago. The report notes that a new programme opened in Uvalde, Texas, which it identifies as Matthew McConaughey's hometown.The report's "2022 by the numbers" page lists 95 instructors, of whom 56 are female, 36 are male, and 3 chose not to identify. It also records 300 volunteers, 170 field trips, 400 game tickets provided and 120 hours of mentoring. The sample programme budget in the report totals $30,000, including $15,000 for personnel, $4,500 for supplies and materials, $3,000 for field trips and events, and $3,000 for operational costs. For fiscal year 2022, the report states that the foundation raised $4,780,000, including $2,900,000 from the Mack, Jack & McConaughey fundraiser. It reports expenditure of $4,349,000, of which $3,961,000 went on programme expenses, $294,000 on administration and business, and $95,000 on fundraising.What impact has the programme had on studentsThe foundation stayed true to its commitment to evaluate the long-term impact of its programmes. Since students joined the programme, it reports that 75% improved their school attendance, 82% improved or maintained their grades, and 99% improved their school behaviour. It also reports that 93% developed more confidence, 100% of students stay in school, and 100% of 12th graders graduate. The report presents these figures alongside statements from students, including Kimberly Romero of Juan Navarro High School, who describes the programme's weekly "Mental Health Monday" reflection time.The report states that the tenth anniversary of the Mack, Jack & McConaughey fundraiser raised more than $10 million to benefit the foundation and four other organisations: Cure Duchenne, Dell Children's, HeartGift Foundation and The Rise School of Austin. In the letter from Camila and Matthew McConaughey, the foundation says that after the Uvalde shooting, which took the lives of 19 children and two teachers, the families it met asked it to "make the loss of these lives matter". The foundation opened a programme at Uvalde High School, set up the Uvalde Relief Fund for grief counselling and other needs, and created the Uvalde Heart Scholarship with Converse for study at Texas A&M University–Corpus Christi.You use AI every day. articles.title: Amid SIR protests, Delhi Police issue body-worn cameras to frontline personnel
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has issued body-worn cameras to officers and personnel deployed on the frontline in the New Delhi area amid allegations of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has issued body-worn cameras to officers and personnel deployed on the frontline in the New Delhi area amid allegations of excesses during recent protests, while a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed before the Delhi high court has sought directions to make body-worn cameras mandatory for Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force (RAF) personnel deployed for crowd control and protests.The bodycams have been issued particularly to personnel involved in crowd management and security arrangements around protest sites and roads leading to the Election Commission of India office, an official source said on Tuesday. Delhi HC PIL seeks mandatory bodycams for police, RAFThe PIL has sought directions making body-worn cameras mandatory for Delhi Police and RAF personnel deployed during protests and crowd-control operations.The plea comes amid heightened scrutiny of police conduct during recent demonstrations in the capital.Delhi Police bodycams to record protest actionA police source said the bodycams would help maintain a real-time video record of events and interactions between police personnel and protesters, besides providing evidence if allegations are made against officers on duty."The bodycams are important, particularly when officers are dealing with large crowds, and there are allegations from either side. The recordings can help establish what happened during a protest," the source said.Bodycams issued amid SIR protests in DelhiThe move comes amid heightened security in the New Delhi, Central Delhi and North Delhi districts following a series of demonstrations against the Election Commission over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.Police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed in large numbers, while multilayer barricades have been placed at several points to prevent protesters from entering restricted areas.Three women journalists allege sexual harassment during protestThe deployment of bodycams assumes significance following complaints of alleged sexual harassment and manhandling made by three women journalists during a protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar at Jantar Mantar on October 2.The journalists alleged that police personnel behaved inappropriately with them. One of the complainants alleged that an officer sexually assaulted her.The New Delhi district police received the complaints and transferred them to the Crime Branch for a fair and impartial inquiry, an officer said.The investigating agency is expected to examine the allegations and record statements of the complainants and other persons concerned.The complaints also led to protests by independent journalists and others outside Parliament Street police station, with demonstrators demanding registration of an FIR and examination of CCTV footage of the alleged incidents.No FIR had been registered in the matter, according to police sources. Police bodycams aimed at improving accountabilityThe use of bodycams is also aimed at strengthening accountability during law-and-order deployments, particularly as police personnel increasingly manage protests involving large groups of political workers, students and civil society members.The recordings could provide investigators with an additional source of evidence while examining complaints against police personnel or allegations of misconduct by protesters, the source said.Delhi Police asks journalists to carry identity cardsDelhi Police has also issued an advisory for journalists covering protests, asking them to carry valid identity cards."Journalists covering protests to carry valid identity cards issued by their respective organisations or valid PIB/DIP accreditation cards, and keep them visibly displayed at all times to facilitate identification by law enforcement at protest sites," the Delhi Police said.In the advisory, police also said media personnel should ensure that their presence or activities do not obstruct police operations or the movement of law enforcement personnel.(With PTI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Jeffrey Archer: The British author who made Indians fall in love with English writing
articles.summary: Archer spent half a century writing about conmen, politicians, tycoons, rogues and impossible comebacks. In the end, none of his protagonists was quite as improbable, indefatigable or entertaining as Jeffrey Archer himself.
articles.body: That Jeffrey Archer had a way with words would be an understatement. In 2019, the only year that he attended the Jaipur Literature Festival, he shared an anecdote that encapsulated the unique position he occupies among Indian readers of English.Archer recalled that a young urchin came up to him with pirated books and asked: “Sir, do you want the latest Jeffrey Archer?” To this, the author replied: “I am the latest Jeffrey Archer.”In that same interaction, he argued that RK Narayan should have won a Nobel Prize and congratulated the Indian team for beating the Aussies Down Under, which came after a session on stage that was filled to the rafters with about 8,000 people.Archer was a prolific writer and one who was more celebrated in India than in his native UK, where his public life often sullied his prowess as a scribe, though even legal misfortune would turn out to be a blessing in literary disguise as he churned out the utterly delightful Prison Diaries about his time navigating Britain’s penal system.As the New York Times lede read: “…a best-selling British author, politician, philanthropist, athlete and one-time jailbird whose résumé seesawed between achievement and disgrace, and who inspired abiding public fascination with headline-grabbing accounts, both fictional and personal, of ambition, self-promotion, misbehaviour and scandal….”In his lifetime, he published 59 works, including 31 novels, 7 short-story collections and numerous other works. Archer’s later novels – perhaps the cut-off date is 2008 – would become a tad too reductive and formulaic. The good characters were, to borrow John Lennon’s lines, classless and free. The bad ones were usually class-conscious gits, and the women were very easily conned.Archer was the sort of writer who was very accessible to the aspirational post-liberalisation middle-class English reader who didn’t have the wherewithal to follow the trials and travails of a Holmes or a Smiley.His writing was more accessible, the vocabulary less grandiose and the literary style compelling without forcing one to grab a dictionary every single time.His last Instagram post hangs like a dangling modifier from the afterlife: “On Saturday 10th October at 7pm I will be discussing my final novel Adam & Eve….”Most great pieces of literary work, at least popular ones, are born out of some form of misfortune. Forsyth wrote The Day of the Jackal upon facing penury after quitting the BBC and living on a friend’s sofa.Similarly, Archer wrote Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less because, well, he was penniless and facing bankruptcy. But the real breakthrough came with Kane and Abel, which sold as many copies as Gone with the Wind and To Kill a Mockingbird. The latter, he recalled, was the “last great book” he read, in an interview with the NYT in which he also admitted that he couldn’t get past page 30 of War and Peace and bragged with his usual braggadocio that Adam and Eve was his “best novel”.Kane and Abel also set the template of the Archer novel, with two Jungian ‘Archer-type’ (pun intended) protagonists who go head-to-head until one of them dies, after which comes a Bollywood-style twist.It was replicated in The Fourth Estate, which was a fictionalised version of the battle between media tycoons Rupert Murdoch and Robert Maxwell, with the latter ostensibly committing suicide in the end. In a cruel twist of fate, his daughter Ghislaine would be best known for her association with convicted paedophile Jeffrey Epstein, who too shuffled off his mortal coil ostensibly of his own accord.Kane and Abel’s follow-up, The Prodigal Daughter, has inspired many, including Angelica Aribam, founder of the Femme First Foundation and former NSUI General Secretary, who wrote on X that Archer’s plot piqued her interest in politics.Over the years, Archer would expand his genre to include art theft, Himalayan expeditions and CIA spy thrillers. His last major works were the Clifton Chronicles, though one must confess one found them rather lacklustre compared to his earlier works.As X user Ritu Chaudhry wrote, his short stories, while not in the same league as the masters of that craft like HH Munro, Anton Chekhov, Isaac Asimov or Edgar Allan Poe – whose are, anyway? – were equally compelling, particularly because one could never guess the twist that came at the end.X user Wordita pointed out, Archer has a unique place among youngsters growing up in post-liberalisation India, along with Enid Blyton, Agatha Christie and John Grisham. One can add Sidney Sheldon to the list for those who were willing to risk their parents’ wrath if they were ever to scour through the pages. Also, as an aside, contrary to popular belief, Sidney Sheldon was born with the XY chromosome, not the XX one.His life, too, had the odd implausibility of an Archer novel. He entered Westminster as a Conservative MP at the age of 29 and seemed destined for a life in politics before losing everything in a fraudulent company, which prompted his first novel.In the 1980s, he was both a best-selling novelist and Margaret Thatcher’s deputy Conservative chairman before being laid low by a sex scandal and later winning damages. But the libel case would return, and an Old Bailey jury convicted him on several charges, which saw him spend two years in jail and became the basis for three bestselling prison diaries.And then he made another comeback, selling more than 300 million books, and remained in the House of Lords until retiring in 2024 and kept on working till the guy in the black robe came calling. His final novel, Adam and Eve, was published the day after he died.Sheridan Morley, one of his oldest friends, once described him as a man who will “dive over a cliff and then be amazed that he’s falling” because in his head, he’s “Peter Pan”.Morley recalled in The Guardian in 2001, in a piece that described him as “mendacious, egotistical, ambitious, pushy, resilient, tactless, gullible, funny, charming, reckless, hard-working, generous, self-obsessed, loyal and naïve”, that he famously convinced he famously persuaded the Beatles to support his Oxfam campaign and brought them to Oxford’s Brasenose College in 1964.That included bypassing their manager Bryan Epstein, and even the Beatles appeared flabbergasted at how they ended up under his charm.At the interval, Morley ran into Ringo Starr, the Beatles drummer, who asked if he knew who this Archer bloke was. Morley replied that everyone was trying to figure out who it was, to which the greatest drummer of all time replied: “He strikes me as a nice enough fella, but he’s the kind of bloke who would bottle your piss and sell it.”As far as epitaphs go, that’s perhaps the best description of the man who rewrote the bestseller charts, moved between Parliament and the peerage, survived financial ruin and tabloid scandal, went from the Old Bailey to Belmarsh, and still emerged to sell hundreds of millions of books around the world. Archer spent half a century writing about conmen, politicians, tycoons, rogues and impossible comebacks. In the end, none of his protagonists was quite as improbable, indefatigable or entertaining as Jeffrey Archer himself.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Childminder who left 27 children alone in her home pleads guilty to neglect
articles.summary: Amanda Mathewson, 55, pleaded guilty to neglect and abandoning children in her care at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court.
articles.body:
A Dunfermline childminder has admitted leaving more than 20 children she was caring for alone and unsupervised in her home.

Amanda Mathewson, 55, pleaded guilty at Kirkcaldy Sheriff Court to neglect and abandoning children in her care.

Her offending took place at a number of locations in Dunfermline and elsewhere in Fife.

The court heard Mathewson had 27 children in her home, 19 more than she was licensed to look after.

Mathewson, who has been a self-employed childminder for 30 years, was arrested by police following allegations of cruelty towards children.

The court heard she had provided childcare services at her home in Dunfermline for children under the age of 16.

At the time of her arrest she had 15 children aged under 12, 10 children under primary school age, and two children under the age of one in her care.

More stories from Edinburgh, Fife & East

Procurator fiscal Vicki Bell told the court two parents became suspicious of Mathewson after being informed their children were not present while the childminder carried out a school run.

They secretly went to the school and found their children were not with Mathewson, despite being in her care.

They then went to her home, where they heard a "child screaming" and found five unattended children in the garden.

One of the children told the witnesses there were no adults inside, and Mathewson had told them to "wait in the garden".

They approached the door of the house to check if there were any adults present, when they hear another child "screaming hysterically" inside.

The door was unlocked, and when the witnesses entered they found a child crying under the kitchen table.

A further nine children, all under five, were found in an upstairs bedroom. Two of them were strapped into prams. The children were said to be "distressed" but uninjured.

Police attended and Mathewson said the children had been left alone for at least 30 minutes.

The court heard ring doorbell footage showed it was the second time that day the children had been left inside the house.

Dirty nappies and hungry, thirsty children

During the police investigation, various children told their parents that being left alone in Mathewson's home was "commonplace".

Some parents told officers that their children became "upset" when they were taken to the childminder's home and those who could talk would say they did not want to go.

The investigation found discrepancies in the number of children in Matthewson's care and the number of children she was seen with on multiple occasions.

For example, Mathewson attended a church Christmas party with three children, despite having nine kids in her care that day.

The parents of the three children who were in attendance were sent a photo of their child with Santa, while the others were just sent a generic photo.

There were other occasions such as a sports day and a visit to Dunfermline fire station where Mathewson was seen with fewer children than she was responsible for.

Parents also raised concerns that their children had not eaten while in the childminder's care due to their clothes staying in "pristine condition" and it was a general theme that their children would return home thirsty.

Some parents also reported their children returned home in dirty nappies or with dry faeces in their underwear.

Court documents state that Mathewson always had loud music playing and did not let parents enter her home at drop off time in an attempt to "conceal how oversubscribed she was".

When the childminder was asked about the number of children in her care, or the whereabouts of certain children she claimed she was being assisted by a "child-minding friend".

Mathewson admitted wilfully neglecting, abandoning and exposing children to a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering or injury to their health.

The court heard she offered childcare places for more children than she could reasonably provide care for at the time.

A Care Inspectorate report published in August 2023 said Mathewson was registered to provide care for a maximum of eight children at any one time.

It included conditions that a maximum of six children could be under the age of 12, no more than three could have started primary school, and no more than one could be under 12-months-old.

The unannounced inspection from about a year before her arrest had rated areas including care, learning and the setting as "very good", the second-highest level in the quality scale.

The report said "children were cared for in a comfortable, welcoming and homely environment" and "were cared for with warmth, kindness and a nurturing approach".

A spokesperson for the Care Inspectorate said this is a "distressing case" and they have "implemented changes as a result of learning from this case."

In a statement given to the BBC, one of the parents said: "The criminal case is important for justice. But our ultimate goal is to ensure no other family has to endure what we have been through. Our trust was broken, but our resolve is not.

"We have turned our pain into a purpose: to rebuild the system of childcare regulation and family support so that it is truly fit to protect Scotland's children."

Sheriff John MacRitchie deferred sentencing until 6 November to allow background reports to be carried out. Mathewson's bail was continued.

articles.title: Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 in Fort Hood shooting, to be executed by firing squad
articles.summary: The former Army major would become the first service member to be executed by firing squad since World War II.
articles.body:
Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad, the Pentagon announced Monday.

"Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell wrote on X .

He added, "The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come."

The U.S. military has not carried out an execution since 1961 and has not used a firing squad to execute a service member since World War II.

The announcement of Trump's approval came days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection. The failed execution prompted Tennessee's governor to halt further executions this year and order a third-party review.

Asked whether the failed execution in Tennessee would lead him to seek changes to capital punishment, Trump called it "an interesting situation." He told reporters in Denton, Texas, that carrying out lethal injections "shouldn't be very difficult."

Trump's approval sets in motion a series of procedural steps toward carrying out Hasan's execution. But Hasan could put the process on hold — potentially for years — by filing a habeas corpus appeal challenging the legality of his detention in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer.

Hasan was convicted in a 2013 court-martial of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder and was sentenced to death. He exhausted his regular appeals in 2025.

What happened in the Fort Hood shooting?

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center, where soldiers were undergoing medical checkups before deploying, and witnesses testified he shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — before he opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He killed 13 people and wounded more than 30.

According to the Associated Press , Hasan said he carried out the shooting to stop soldiers from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims.

He represented himself at his 2013 court-martial and mounted little defense, telling jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides."

The Pentagon did not explain why Hasan would be executed by firing squad rather than lethal injection, the method specified in the military's current execution regulations. It also did not say whether those regulations would need to change.

The Army adopted a plan in February for carrying out military executions at the federal government's execution facility in Terre Haute, Ind., ABC News reported in June.

Known as Operation Resolute Justice, the plan calls for condemned service members to be transferred there from the military prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., and for the Army to coordinate with the Federal Bureau of Prisons. The Army is to be ready to carry out an execution no sooner than 60 days and within 150 days of presidential approval. ABC's report did not specify an execution method.

The Justice Department separately directed the Bureau of Prisons in April to expand its protocol for federal civilian executions to include methods beyond lethal injection, including firing squads. That change does not apply to military executions.

Firing squads have also recently returned at the state level. Five states allow them, according to the Death Penalty Information Center : Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.

Idaho made the firing squad its primary execution method on July 1 after a law signed in 2025 took effect. South Carolina carried out three firing squad executions in 2025, the first uses of the method in the U.S. since 2010. Condemned prisoners there can choose among authorized execution methods.

After Pike's failed execution, several top Republicans in Tennessee said they want to explore alternative ways of executing condemned prisoners.

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, told the AP , "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully."

Top legislative leaders have already spoken with Blackburn about potential changes to state execution laws during their 2027 session.

"We want to broaden it, include more methods," Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton said. "What those are as of today, I'm not sure. But I don't think there's any method that's off the table at this point."

Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions are even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kan.

President George W. Bush approved the execution of Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008, but a judge put it on hold. Gray remains at Fort Leavenworth.

The last person executed under the military justice system was Pvt. John Bennett, who was hanged in 1961 for the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl.

articles.title: Jade Thirlwall and Hans Zimmer team up for Blue Planet III song
articles.summary: The ex-Little Mix star worked with Hans Zimmer on an official track for the BBC nature documentary.
articles.body:
Singer Jade Thirlwall says working on the official song for BBC documentary Blue Planet III is "one of the best things" she's ever done.

The former Little Mix star worked with legendary composer Hans Zimmer on Into The Deep (Seas Cry), a piece created for the launch of the series narrated by Sir David Attenborough.

Thirlwall, who debuted the track on BBC Radio 1's Breakfast Show, told host Greg James working on it was a "very special" experience.

Blue Planet III is due to air this autumn, but an official release date is yet to be announced.

During her breakfast show appearance, Thirlwall said Blue Planet, which focuses on the life of our seas and oceans, was her favourite TV show.

"When this opportunity came in, I might have shed a little tear," she said.

"I was just so buzzing to be a part of something so special.

"I'm a huge David Attenborough fan, I love the planet, I love the oceans. It was so magical getting to write a song all about that."

Thirlwall said the track, which mixes her striking vocals with Hans Zimmer's signature orchestral builds, was written to be "celebratory".

She said footage captured by Blue Planet III crews played in the background as she worked on creating the theatrical piece.

"The song is about the oceans and how special they are, hope, fighting the good fight to make the world a better place," she said.

Thirlwall also said she was "busy writing" a second album after a busy summer of festival performances, including slots at Reading and Leeds in August.

It's not the first time a big artist has worked with Hans Zimmer to create a track for the BBC's nature programmes.

Singer RAYE and Bastille frontman Dan Smith have previously collaborated with the Oscar-winner.

George Fenton, another key Blue Planet composer who'd worked on other BBC nature documentaries, as well as classic films such as Gandhi and Groundhog Day, died this week at the age of 76.

articles.title: Italy PM Giorgia Meloni files to protect her voice from AI deepfakes
articles.summary: Giorgia Meloni submitted a four-second audio to a EU agency in a bid to protect her voice from deepfakes.
articles.body:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has applied to trademark her voice in a move to protect herself against artificial intelligence (AI) deepfakes.

The application to the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) was made on Monday and can be found on their website . The prime minister's office also confirmed the application.

As part of it, Meloni recorded a four-second audio where she says "Io sono Giorgia" - I am Giorgia Meloni" in Italian - twice.

Meloni is not alone in filing to protect her identity from unauthorised use by AI platforms. In January, US actor Matthew McConaughey led the way by trademarking his image and voice.

Singer Taylor Swift did similar in April, submitting three trademark applications in the US - one using a photo of herself on stage during her Eras Tour, and the other two being audio clips of her introducing herself while promoting her last album.

In August, more than 80 performers called on British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to introduce legislation which would give every person in the UK a legal right to own their voice.

Actors including Matt Lucas, Hugh Bonneville and Nicola Coughlan were among those calling for greater protection against their voices being used by AI.

Voice clones are created by training AI on recordings of real people. Quick versions can be made from a few seconds of audio, but high-quality copycats tend to require hours.

Meloni's decision to trademark her voice comes ahead of Italy's general elections next year.

The phrase, "Io sono Giorgia", was the title of Meloni's 2021 autobiography and is associated with the prime minister's political campaigns.

In 2024, Meloni sought €100,000 (£84,920) in damages after deepfake porn videos of her were uploaded online.

A deepfake image is one where the face of one person is digitally added to the body of another. In recent years, deepfake porn has become commonplace on the internet and victims have spoken out about the trauma it has caused them.

More recently, in May this year, Meloni warned of the dangers of deepfakes as several AI-generated images of her wearing lingerie were circulating online.

In a post on social media, Meloni added: "The point, however, goes beyond me. Deepfakes are a dangerous tool, because they can deceive, manipulate, and strike anyone. I can defend myself. Many others cannot."

articles.title: Musician Tom Grennan returns to Bedford venue for free shows
articles.summary: The Little Bit of Love singer will play gigs at the venue where he performed as a teenager.
articles.body:
Singer-songwriter Tom Grennan has organised two free gigs at the music venue where he began performing as a teenager.

The Bedford-born musician is playing three venues over three days on his Looking Back Live tour, featuring what promoters described as "intimate acoustic sets in the rooms that helped shape his journey".

Tickets for the Little Bit Of Love singer's two shows at Bedford Esquires have already been allocated through an online lottery.

Venue owner Gareth Barber said: "We watched him grow as a young teen in local bands to the genuine star he has become and I'm really proud of how far he has gone."

Grennan has regularly returned to Esquires, where he frequently performed during his teenage years, while promoting his three number one albums.

Earlier this year he also headlined a concert at Bedford Park as part of the Bedford Summer Sessions.

Barber said: "He always possessed a unique voice and talent, but his hard work and dedication to being the best he can be is a testament to his character and serves as a blueprint for any aspiring local musician."

The tour began at The Finsbury in London on Monday, and Grennan will play the final two shows at O'Connell's in Manchester on Wednesday.

Promoters DICE have encouraged attendees to donate money on entry to each venue which will "go directly towards supporting these vital grassroots music spaces".

articles.title: Rosie O'Donnell and Julie Hesmondhalgh lead cast of The Pelicot Trial play
articles.summary: The four-hour one-off performance will also star Adjoa Andoh and Juliet Stevenson and
articles.body:
US comedian Rosie O'Donnell, Celebrity Traitors star Julie Hesmondhalgh, Bridgerton's Adjoa Andoh and EastEnders actress Tamzin Outhwaite will appear in a play based on the trial of the husband of Gisele Pelicot.

Thirty actors and public figures will take part in The Pelicot Trial, a one-off "documentary theatre" style performance at London's County Hall next month.

The play has been created from documents from the trial and psychiatric reports of dozens of men who were prosecuted in the case, which caused outrage in France and around the world, and turned Gisele Pelicot into a symbol of strength against sexual assault.

Dominique Pelicot was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping his then wife, and allowing 50 other men to rape her while she was unconscious.

Other cast members include Truly, Madly, Deeply star Juliet Stevenson, All Creatures Great and Small actor Samuel West, Sixth Sense's Oliva Wiliams and Slow Horses' Kadiff Kirwan.

Comedian Rosie Jones, Dune actress Sharon Duncan-Brewster, Bridgerton's Lorraine Ashbourne and Rizzle Kicks rapper Jordan Stephens will also take part.

Further casting for the four-hour play, which was developed in collaboration with journalists and feminist organisations in France, will be announced in the coming weeks.

The Pelicot Trial will be staged by the Young Vic theatre at London's County Hall on 30 November, and will also be streamed online.

The Young Vic said the performance is a "profoundly affecting piece of documentary theatre, comprised of testimonies and written accounts from the trial, (which) pays tribute to the ordinary woman who opened the way to change".

Gisele Pelicot, 73, waived her right to anonymity as a survivor of sexual abuse, and said shame should fall on her abusers, not her.

The Pelicot Trial received its world premiere in Vienna last year and has since toured to cities including Avignon, New York, Lisbon, Milan and Bergen.

Tickets for the London performance will go on general sale on Wednesday.

articles.title: Ghana arrests seven women over cedi 'money bouquets'
articles.summary: The arrests are part of the country's efforts to curb the misuse and abuse of the national currency.
articles.body:
Ghanaian authorities have arrested seven people for allegedly using banknotes to make so-called "money bouquets" and decorate cakes.

The Bank of Ghana says the practice is illegal and amounts to misuse and improper handling of the cedi, the national currency.

The arrests, carried out in collaboration with the police, followed a tip-off that led to a swoop on the suspects, all women, accused of selling the bouquets in different parts of the capital, Accra.

The arrests are the biggest enforcement of the law against misusing the currency. In July, the bank issued a notice warning this could amount to an offence.

It warned against "acts that tend to depreciate or impair the national currency, including any conduct that undermines its lawful value or use".

Bouquets of banknotes or cakes decorated with currency are often ordered as gifts for weddings, birthdays, graduations and other celebrations.

The police have launched investigations, and the authorities say the suspects will be prosecuted. They could face a fine or jail term, to be determined by the court.

Dinah Bonzi, an official in the Bank of Ghana's currency department, said anyone aiding or promoting such activities could also be arrested and prosecuted.

''The Ghana cedi is legal tender… and must be treated with respect. The misuse or abuse of the currency is an offence and may attract sanctions under the law,'' she said.

"Today's arrest should serve as a clear warning to the public. Let us all handle the Ghana cedi with dignity."

The central bank has repeatedly warned against activities such as "spraying" - or throwing money at events such as weddings - writing on or altering notes and using them in decorations such as floral-like bouquets in weddings, birthdays and other occasions.

The use of money decorations has become more common in Ghana in recent years, with the practice also gaining a foothold in other African countries.

In recent years authorities in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Botswana have also issued warnings against misusing the national currencies.

articles.title: George Lucas began buying California ranchland in 1978; the holdings expanded to nearly 5,000 acres, with a 50,000-square-foot main house, more than a dozen buildings, and Skywalker Sound at its core
articles.summary: First, it was just a dairy ranch tucked away in a quiet Marin County valley.
articles.body: First, it was just a dairy ranch tucked away in a quiet Marin County valley. Today, it is a 4,700-acre moviemaking retreat, with its own fire brigade, a vineyard and a lake named after the Ewoks!In 1978, filmmaker George Lucas bought the first parcel of what would eventually become Skywalker Ranch, using money he had made from Star Wars. All he wanted was a private filmmaking haven away from Hollywood. Nearly five decades later, that idea has grown into a sprawling creative compound with more than a dozen buildings, a 50,000-square-foot main house and Skywalker Sound at its heart. But despite its futuristic name, the ranch looks like an old Northern California estate, with Victorian architecture, gardens, farmland and handcrafted details woven into the landscape.“I've never been into science fiction,” the creator of Star Wars told AD. His penchant for Victorian and Mission architecture is evident on the ranch. “My taste has always been romantic. I think my heart lies at about the year 1910. I love that style.” The ranch is also home to his Skywalker Sound facility, an extensive research library.A Victorian-style house at the centreThe centrepiece is a Victorian-style main house finished in 1985. The main house spans 50,000 square feet, more than an acre under one roof, according to the LA Times. Lucas does not live there. It is a space dedicated to his work and business meetings. “I’ve always worked out of my house. I think a lot of writers do. It’s just a much more friendly atmosphere, more comfortable and calming. I wanted a nice, quiet place to come up with ideas, because, really, we’re in the ideas business. So when I got the opportunity and the wherewithal to do it, I thought, Well, I’m going to do it myself,” he told the outlet.The creamy white house was designed in the style of a grand Victorian residence, complete with turrets, verandas, stained glass and fireplaces. Lucas also did his filmmaker thing. He created a fictional history for the building. In his version, it was built in 1869 and extended in 1910 with a library wing in the style of the architects Greene and Greene. To make it look real, he set up an art-glass studio and a mill shop on the grounds. Hired craftsmen built the staircase and stained-glass windows there. “I've always been a frustrated architect. But I couldn't get past the maths,” he said. Nothing here is accidental.The ranch also has a research library. It has a leaded-glass dome and redwood shelves made from timber salvaged from an old bridge. Lucas bought the book collections of both Paramount and Universal. The shelves cover military history, costumes and insects, along with a large geography section.Skywalker SoundIn 1987, Skywalker Sound moved onto the ranch. It operates from the Technical Building beside Lake Ewok. It is a building dressed up to look like an ivy-covered brick winery. The studio, set against the backdrop of picturesque mountains, is a dream place for the technicians as well. “In the morning, there’s mist coming up from Ewok Lake, and there’s dew on everything. It’s kind of crazy-beautiful. It looks like a very well-shot movie, just driving up to it,” award-winning sound designer and re-recording mixer Bonnie Wild, who started work at the studio in 2012, said.Directors have long used the place as a retreat. James Cameron, Philip Kaufman and Clint Eastwood are among the visitors to Skywalker Sound. The guests stay at an on-site inn where rooms are themed after people Lucas admires. The John Ford room allows smoking because, well, Ford smoked. The Frank Lloyd Wright room displays a rare Wright drawing of a resort that was never built. The inn is the place where art meets comfort.The ranch also has three restaurants, a 35-seater theatre and a health club with yoga and Pilates classes. An organic garden, olive grove and vineyard add to the feeling of a self-contained rural community. The grounds are also home to horses, goats, chickens, Texas longhorns and even a Vietnamese pot-bellied pig named Betty Boop.Nearly five decades after Lucas began assembling the land, the ranch remains one of the most unusual filmmaking environments in the world. It is a working studio, a retreat and an architectural fantasy, with hints of the past that Lucas always wanted to inhabit.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: British national arrested in connection with RAF Fairford incident
articles.summary: It is the seventh arrest in connection to the incident near RAF Fairford last month.
articles.body:
A 22-year-old British national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident close to RAF Fairford, counter-terror police said.

He was arrested in Westminster, London, on Tuesday as part of the investigation into the incident near the airbase in Gloucestershire on 27 September.

It is the seventh arrest in connection to the incident but no one has been charged.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.

Senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said it "remains a live investigation" and police are continuing to "pursue multiple lines of enquiry".

Five men were arrested on 27 September near the base in the connection with the incident and were subsequently released on police bail.

The men, aged between 23 and 25, were detained in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual Iranian-British national, was arrested on 1 October in Westminster and was also later released on bail.

RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used by the US Air Force for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

On Sunday, it emerged the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details.

While speaking to a group of reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.

He replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.

"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy.

"But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."

Earlier, US Vice-President JD Vance said the bombers were moved "out of an abundance of caution".

The comments came after US media reports suggested the decision was made after intelligence suggested Iran was plotting a drone attack. The BBC has not verified those reports.

On Tuesday, a spokesperson for US European Command, which coordinated American military activity in Europe, said it would be "inappropriate to discuss matters of intelligence" but that the US would "continue to assess the threat environment" at bases.

The spokesperson added the US remains at the "highest state of readiness" and would take "appropriate actions to protect our people, our platforms, and the bases where our forces operate".

Prior to Trump's intervention on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to his previous comments, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.

articles.title: Deaf couple's Southampton home rebuilt by DIY SOS volunteers
articles.summary: The Alis' home rebuild is being shown on the BBC show after they lost £72,000 on building work.
articles.body:
A profoundly deaf couple, whose home was left unsafe by unfinished building work, will see it being transformed by hundreds of volunteers when the latest episode of DIY SOS is broadcast.

Ahmed and Rifat Ali, from Bitterne in Southampton, lost £72,000 on a ground floor extension which was halted and later condemned.

The couple and their three children were left living upstairs, unable to use their kitchen or garden, until the hit BBC show's team rebuilt the house last October.

The episode, which reveals technology designed to help the couple run their home, will be on BBC One and iPlayer at 20:00 BST.

DIY SOS designer Gaby Blackman said: "All we hear about in our community is division and that is not what we found. We found a united, kind, warm community all really just trying to help a family in need."

More than 150 tradespeople turned up on the first day of the build, with presenter Nick Knowles saying the team had to do "six months work in about seven days".

Before work began, Ahmed, speaking through an interpreter, told volunteers: "It's been quite a dark period and I just feel like this is the light at the end of the tunnel."

Rifat said: "I can't believe that you're going to change our house and make it home again. We just can't wait to come back. So thank you from the bottom of our hearts."

The couple said that because they were deaf and their children could hear, having lots of walls in the house was a barrier, and they hoped for clear lines of sight.

Show electrician Billy Byrne said alarms would use different coloured flashing lights to tell the parents which part of the house had a problem, describing the system as "revolutionary".

Stuart Hanlon, whose company donated the technology, said display panels would also show a blue light if one of the children left the taps running.

He said of the house before the work: "I have never seen anything that dangerous. One wrong step and it would have been a very different story."

Furniture maker Radha Sivyer, who redesigned the bedroom shared by the couple's two sons, said: "We're not making things to look pretty for TV. We're actually building real, meaningful, changed homes."

Neighbours said the build had brought the street closer, with a roast dinner for residents at a spiritualist church and a new WhatsApp group.

Electrician Tom, from Portsmouth, said the volunteers, many of whom came from Portsmouth, Gosport and Southampton, had formed "a strong band of brothers" who now help each other find work.

Knowles said that long after people had forgotten who he was, the homes the show had built would "still be looking after people".

articles.title: In 1984, Patrick Swayze bought a 4.5-acre ranch outside Los Angeles and built it into an Arabian-horse retreat with a 16-stall barn, two arenas and a dance studio; after his death, it sold for $2.9 million and later listed for $4.5 million

articles.body: American actor and dancer Patrick Swayze spent much of his career moving between Hollywood sets and the dance floor. Away from both, he and his wife, Lisa Niemi, built a very different kind of retreat in California. A 4.5-acre ranch where they bred and rode Arabian horses and created dedicated spaces for both equestrian activities and dance.Known as Rancho Bizarro, the property in the San Fernando Valley included a 16-stall barn, two arenas, a round yard, and a dance studio. Decades after Swayze and Niemi bought the property, it returned to the market with a $4.5 million asking price. An entity tied to philanthropist and oil heiress Aileen Getty had bought the ranch from Niemi for $2.9 million in 2015, Mansion Global reported.The ranch Patrick Swayze built around horses and danceSwayze and Niemi bought the 4.5-acre property in the 1980s and developed it into an equestrian estate. In a 1997 interview, Swayze described the setup as including a 16-stall barn, a round yard and two arenas. The couple also spent their free time breeding and riding Arabian horses.The property sits in Sylmar, in Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley, behind gates at the end of a cul-de-sac. It combines a 1940s ranch-style house with equestrian facilities and a guest cottage. The main residence covers about 3,516 square feet and has three bedrooms and five bathrooms.The house still holds Swayze's dance studio. The space has mirrored walls and enough room to serve as a rehearsal area.The house includes a living room with exposed beams and a fireplace, while the kitchen opens towards a glass-enclosed atrium overlooking the grounds and swimming pool. The property also includes covered outdoor areas, a guest cottage and a detached garage.The equestrian section includes a barn with horse stalls, a tack room, laundry facilities and grooming areas, along with a riding arena. The listing also mentioned two goats, Cocoa and Caramel, and two ducks named Baby and Johnny.From $2.9 million sale to $4.5 million listingNiemi sold Rancho Bizarro to an entity connected to Aileen Getty in 2015 for $2.9 million, according to property records cited by Mansion Global. Getty is a philanthropist and oil heiress, and the ranch remained associated with her ownership when it was listed for $4.5 million in 2023.The $4.5 million asking price represented a $1.6 million increase over the property's 2015 sale price.Who was Patrick Swayze?Swayze rose to global fame with Dirty Dancing in 1987, playing dance instructor Johnny Castle opposite Jennifer Grey. He followed that success with films including Road House in 1989 and Ghost in 1990. He also starred in the 1991 action film Point Break.Dance remained an important part of Swayze's life beyond his screen roles. He was a trained ballet dancer, and his work with Niemi extended into their shared interest in horses and equestrian activities.Swayze and Niemi married on June 12, 1975, and remained together until his death in September 2009. Swayze died at 57 after battling pancreatic cancer.Swayze also had a connection to music through Dirty Dancing. He co-wrote and performed the song "She's Like the Wind" for the film's soundtrack, which became a hit in 1987. articles.title: Iranian men accused of spying targeted journalists for 'serious violence', court hears
articles.summary: The prosecution says the targets were journalists working for a satellite channel critical of the Iranian government.
articles.body:
Three Iranian men have gone on trial in London accused of spying for Iran on UK-based journalists, who were being targeted so "serious violence" could be inflicted on them.

The prosecution said Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, was to carry out the attack, with Farhad Manesh, 46, and Shapoor Noori, 57, doing the surveillance and reconnaissance. All three were born in Iran but were living in London.

The jury at Woolwich Crown Court heard that Sepahvand does not deny his involvement but said he did it out of fear of the consequences of refusing.

The prosecution said that is "an entirely bogus claim", adding that he did it for money and to have a criminal conviction for theft in Iran "fixed".

Sepahvand was in contact with two men with Iranian telephone numbers.

According to the prosecution, Manesh and Noori are expected to say they did not know they were carrying out surveillance on behalf of Iran.

All three face charges under the National Security Act, including "assisting a foreign intelligence service".

Prosecutor Bill Emlyn Jones KC said the men's targets were journalists working for Iran International - a Persian-language satellite channel that is critical of the Tehran regime and has its headquarters in London.

Jones said at least two journalists linked to Iran International were targeted in the surveillance.

He said at least one of them was to be "subjected to serious violence" as retribution and "to try to silence and deter others who might dare to voice their criticism".

Iran International, which broadcasts into Iran, has been declared as a "terrorist organisation" by Tehran.

"The evidence we will call illustrates that these three defendants carried out surveillance and reconnaissance, visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos, taking videos, doing online research about them," Jones said.

"The defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying," he added.

The men also allegedly had a "briefing sheet" on a barrister, Jonathan Turner, who was a founding member of a group called UK Lawyers for Israel.

One Iran International journalist who was allegedly targeted was Mojtaba Pourmohsen.

Images of him, his workplace and a hotel where he had lived were found in a "briefing document" on Sepahvand's mobile phone.

The prosecution says Noori took pictures of the block of flats Pourmohsen lived in in Brentford, southwest London, in December 2024.

It is also alleged that Sepahvand and Manesh went there to take photos and videos.

Jones said Sepahvand's motivation was to try to resolve a criminal conviction he had in Iran for theft.

"He was not just in it for money. He quite explicitly wants something very particular in return for his work - he wanted his criminal conviction in Iran to be fixed," Jones told the jury.

The three men, who each had an interpreter in the dock, deny all the charges.

All three were granted temporary leave to remain in the UK after claiming asylum. They arrived in the UK between 2016 and 2022.

Sepahvand arrived in 2016 concealed in a lorry. The other two arrived in small boats.

articles.title: In 2021, Arnold Schwarzenegger donated $250,000 to help homeless veterans in Los Angeles; before Christmas, 25 tiny shelters were installed with beds, climate control and doors residents could lock
articles.summary: In 2021, Arnold Schwarzenegger donated $250,000 to help provide tiny shelters for homeless veterans in Los Angeles.
articles.body: In 2021, Arnold Schwarzenegger donated $250,000 to help provide tiny shelters for homeless veterans in Los Angeles. By Christmas, 25 shelters purchased through his donation had been installed at the Veterans Affairs campus in West Los Angeles, giving former service members a temporary place to stay as they worked towards more stable housing.According to Fox 11, the former California governor made the donation to Village for Vets, a non-profit organisation that works with the Greater Los Angeles VA Healthcare System to support veterans and their families. The money helped the organisation purchase 25 shelters for veterans who had been living on the streets.After the shelters were installed by Team Rubicon volunteers, Schwarzenegger visited the site and met some of the veterans who were staying there. His visit came shortly before Christmas and included a tour of the shelters as well as a holiday event for residents.“I’m really ecstatic. To me, this is the greatest Christmas gift!” Schwarzenegger told Fox 11 while standing inside one of the shelters.What the tiny shelters offeredThe shelters were intended as temporary accommodation rather than permanent homes. Village for Vets said its Tiny Shelter Program was designed to give homeless veterans a safer and more comfortable place to live while they worked towards housing stability.Each small shelter provided a roof, climate control, a comfortable bed and a door that residents could lock. Village for Vets said these basic facilities represented an improvement over living in tent encampments and gave veterans greater safety and dignity.The need for protection from the weather was particularly clear during Schwarzenegger’s visit, which took place on a rainy day in Los Angeles. “It proves the point they are going through not just sunshine and wonderful weather,” Schwarzenegger said.Rob Reynolds of AMVets, a long-time advocate for veterans in West Los Angeles, said the shelters offered facilities that could make a meaningful difference to people moving off the streets. “They have electricity, they have heating and air conditioning, helps bring a little bit of pride back,” Reynolds said.Veteran calls shelter a ‘life-saver’Among the residents Schwarzenegger met was veteran Bruce Henry Cooper, who personally thanked the former governor for helping fund the shelters. “It’s been a life-saver for me,” Cooper said.For Cooper, Schwarzenegger’s involvement also sent a message that veterans facing homelessness had not been overlooked. “He has not forgotten us. Not forgotten anybody,” Cooper said.Village for Vets said the shelters were an important step in helping homeless veterans move towards stable housing. The organisation made clear that the small structures were not meant to be a permanent answer to homelessness.Instead, the programme provided temporary shelter for veterans on their journey towards housing stability. By giving residents a bed, climate control, a roof and a locking door, the organisation said the shelters offered an improved standard of living compared with tent encampments.Schwarzenegger visits veterans before ChristmasSchwarzenegger also spoke about the project in a message shared by Village for Vets after the shelters were installed. “Today, I celebrated Christmas early. The 25 homes I donated for homeless veterans were installed here in LA. It was fantastic to spend some time with our heroes and welcome them into their new homes,” he said.His son Patrick Schwarzenegger joined him during the visit. At a barbecue held as part of the event for veterans, Patrick handed out MOSH nutrition bars. “We owe everything to our veterans, they’ve sacrificed their lives, their family hoods for us and our freedom,” Patrick Schwarzenegger said.He added, “Its the holidays, anything we can do to make other people’s week a little better and happier. It’s all good.”For Arnold Schwarzenegger, the donation was also connected to his own experience in the United States and his desire to give something back to the country. “It makes me feel good I can give something back to this country that has given everything to me,” he said.The impact of Schwarzenegger’s contribution also extended beyond the 25 shelters, according to Village for Vets. The organisation said that after his donation became public, it received more than $100,000 in additional contributions from over 120 new donors. articles.title: North Yorkshire Airbnbs will not be exempt from tourist tax - mayor
articles.summary: Only applying it to hotels would be "disgraceful", says councillor.
articles.body:
The mayor of York and North Yorkshire has promised he would not introduce an overnight visitor levy unless it applied to the entire accommodation sector.

Regional mayors in England are set to gain powers to impose what has been dubbed a "tourist tax" as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.

During a meeting last week, Whitby councillor Neil Swannick said it would be "disgraceful" if Airbnbs and holiday lets were exempt.

The region's mayor, David Skaith, agreed, telling him: "I won't introduce it if it doesn't touch Airbnb."

The idea was first raised under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in November and is similar to schemes running in Scotland and European destinations.

Skaith said discussions were continuing with the government about how a levy could operate in practice, the Local Democray Reporting Service reports .

No decision has yet been made on whether to introduce a visitor levy in York and North Yorkshire, with further consultation expected before any final proposals are brought forward.

A report previously recommended imposing a £1 per night tourist tax over a percentage-based model due to its simplicity and predictable revenue.

It said potential exemptions could be made for low-cost stays to reduce the burden on small operators and campsites.

Swannick said the levy must apply equally to all forms of visitor accommodation.

"I think it would be absolutely disgraceful if this tax were to be imposed on hotels, but not on the Airbnbs and holiday lets," he said.

Skaith told councillors the scheme could help fund improvements communities had repeatedly requested.

"We want to see improved transport, we want to see our high streets regenerated and all these kinds of things," he said.

"We've got an opportunity to collect a very small amount of money per night to have a large amount of money that we can put into the region and invest in places like Scarborough, Whitby and Filey."

Alison Hume, Labour MP for Scarborough and Whitby, said businesses wanted "real and quantifiable answers" about how a levy would operate and whether its benefits would outweigh the costs.

She said at a recent meeting: "The overwhelming view was that introducing a levy on stays in our coastal communities during a time of high utility bills, staff costs and VAT at 20%, this levy could potentially be the straw that breaks the camel's back."

Whitby councillor Phil Trumper was also critical of the proposal and said: "It's just another tax, in my opinion.

"It will create unemployment in towns like Whitby."

It comes as the government is preparing to introduce a mandatory national register for short-term holiday lets and Airbnb-style accommodation from March 2027.

articles.title: UK to make last-ditch effort to stop Israel closing East Jerusalem consulate
articles.summary: Israel has threatened to close the consulate, which handles UK relations with Palestinians in the city, over British sanctions on Israeli settlements.
articles.body:
The UK government is making a last-ditch attempt to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.

Israel said in September that it would shut the mission, which is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv, in retaliation for the UK announcing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

British sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.

The Foreign Office said it would not comment on "speculation and live discussions" that the UK could expel Israeli diplomats in response.

The Israeli government said it would close the mission within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement, meaning that the mission - first established in 1838 - will close on Thursday unless a deal is reached.

The consulate handles UK relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.

UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week for talks but seemingly left without reaching an agreement.

According to Israeli media, the UK is threatening to expel up to 27 Israeli diplomats if the closure goes ahead.

Such a tit-for-tat expulsion of diplomats is more common among adversaries than allies.

France and Canada joined the UK in the initial sanctions, but Israel has not taken action against them.

Emily Thornberry, chair of the foreign affairs committee, said: "Beyond the fact that the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem - occupied Palestinian territory - is not in Israel's prerogative, it is yet another attempt by this far-right Israeli government to block a two-state solution."

She added: "It is illegal, and the UK must resist it."

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has previously said that they do not want the consulate to close.

"It would damage the very important work that we are doing, helping people in those communities," he said last month.

articles.title: A Colorado ranch homesteaded before statehood stayed with the same family for six generations; more than 150 years later, 650 of its roughly 700 acres were permanently protected from subdivision
articles.summary: The Hutchinson Ranch, a historic family-owned property in Colorado, has successfully secured conservation easements to protect 650 of its 700 acres from subdivision, ensuring the family legacy continues for generations to come.
articles.body: The 700-acre Hutchinson Ranch along US Highway 50 between Salida and Poncha Springs, recognised as the oldest family-owned ranch in Colorado’s Upper Arkansas Valley, is now largely protected from development.The ranch has been in the Hutchinson family for six generations. In 2013, conservation agreements covering 650 acres were completed, blocking subdivision while keeping ownership and ranching with the family, according to The Trust for Public Land.The ranch dates back to 1868Joseph Sykes Hutchinson and his wife, Annabel McPherson Hutchinson, first homesteaded part of the property in 1868.At the time, Colorado was still a US territory. The territory became a state eight years later, in 1876.Joseph had arrived in Colorado in 1866 after being wounded during the Battle of Vicksburg in the Civil War. The family soon built a large cattle operation. By the 1870s, the Hutchinsons had more than 5,000 cattle spread across parts of Colorado.Its historic value was recognised in 2003, when the ranch and its original homestead were included among Colorado Preservation Inc.'s top five most endangered properties.The Hutchinsons later donated the original homestead to the Town of Poncha Springs. The historic property is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.Why 650 acres were protectedThe Hutchinsons wanted to keep the ranch together, but conservation groups offered another way to protect the land without the family having to give up ownership.A conservation easement is essentially a permanent legal agreement that limits what can be done with a property. In this case, it means the protected parts of the ranch cannot be split into smaller parcels for development.The first 180 acres were protected in 2010 after the Hutchinson family donated a conservation easement to the Land Trust of Upper Arkansas.The Trust for Public Land later bought the development rights to another 470 acres. Those agreements were completed in 2011 and 2013 and are held by the Colorado Cattlemen's Agricultural Land Trust.Together, the agreements protected 650 acres of the approximately 700-acre ranch.The family did not have to sell the land. It could continue owning the ranch, raising cattle and passing the property to future generations.The project was supported by Great Outdoors Colorado, the Natural Resources Conservation Service, Chaffee County and the Colorado Parks & Wildlife Habitat Protection Program.Six generations of HutchinsonsAbby Hutchinson, the granddaughter of family patriarch Wendell “Doc” Hutchinson, took on the job of managing the ranch and its cattle operation.Wendell was born in 1924 and spent most of his life on the ranch. He left for college and served during World War II, but later returned to the family property.After his father, Mills Hutchinson, died in 1949, Wendell and his wife, Mary Sue Swallow, took over the ranch. Keeping it running was not easy. Wendell also worked as a veterinarian and used that income to help support the ranch.He became well known in the local community. He served on the Salida school board for 29 years and led the Chaffee County 4-H Livestock Club for 16 years. articles.title: AfD candidate Rausch elected speaker of German regional parliament for first time
articles.summary: Although Tobias Rausch's role is largely symbolic, opponents have described the result as a watershed moment.
articles.body:
A month after Germany's far-right AfD scored a decisive victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, the party's candidate Tobias Rausch has been elected as parliament speaker there too.

Not since World War Two has a far-right party secured the post of speaker, and protesters outside the building in Magdeburg held up banners saying, "Never again is now".

Although the AfD fell three seats short of a majority in last month's election, Rausch, 35, comfortably won Tuesday's vote with the support of 9 MPs from other parties.

"The days of political firewalls should be a thing of the past," Rausch said after the vote, rejecting a post-war consensus in German politics not to work with the far right.

This was the first time since last month's state vote that Saxony-Anhalt's newly elected representatives had gathered in parliament, and regional Greens party leader Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz said "a line has been crossed" with the election of a far-right speaker of parliament, and it was a watershed moment.

"We will not let ourselves be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights are curtailed either here or for people in the state," she said.

The AfD is considered pro-Russian and anti-immigrant, with plans to segregate child refugees in schools, as well as intolerant towards the LGBT community.

Within Saxony-Anhalt it is also classed as "right-wing extremist" by domestic intelligence, a description rejected by party leaders. Until now its members have sat on the right fringe of the state parliament, but ahead of Tuesday's inaugural session it successfully argued that it should now sit in the centre.

Rausch, a trained estate agent, has been a member of the parliament for 10 years and he is seen as a close confidant of local AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund, a charismatic figure who is now seeking to become state premier in December.

His new role is largely symbolic, but Rausch will now chair debates, have the power to control access to the parliament building and represent parliament at official events.

Although his victory was secured by five MPs from the hard-left BSW, there was surprise that four other unidentified MPs also voted for Rausch. Commentators immediately asked if he had secured the backing of members of the conservative CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has ruled out working with the AfD.

Fourteen of the CDU's state MPs took part in the vote, but only five of them abstained as planned, and one unconfirmed report suggested four may have backed Rausch. Ahead of the vote, all 15 had ruled out voting for the AfD.

Outside parliament, more than 300 protesters voiced their anger at the AfD's victory, and they crowded around Ulrich Siegmund as he spoke to German media.

Siegmund's bid to become state premier is by no means secure. Like Rauch he will need the backing of 42 MPs in the 83-seat legislature.

The BSW has refused to enter into a coalition with the AfD and has said it would instead back a non-partisan candidate for state premier and abstain in December's vote.

articles.body: Kolkata: The Bengal govt has allocated a record Rs 407 crore in subsidy for its agricultural mechanisation scheme in 2026-27, aiming to boost the rural economy, promote technology-driven farming and create employment opportunities for rural youth.Agriculture minister Dudh Kumar Mondal said the allocation was the highest under the scheme. “The govt has steadily increased financial support for technological development in agriculture. articles.title: Nurses suspend stir after talks
articles.summary: Tamil Nadu mid-level nurses suspend hunger strike after talks with health secretary; seek permanent jobs, equal pay, ₹45,000 salary, pending incentives, warn Nov 3 protest.
articles.body: Chennai: Nurses of the Tamil Nadu Mid-Level Healthcare Providers’ Union suspended their hunger strike after a three-hour meeting with health secretary Darez Ahamed on Monday, following protests for a pay hike and permanent jobs. The union said it would resume the agitation across from Nov 3 if the govt failed to fulfil its assurances.Union president N Sundari said the govt had promised the nurses that most of their demands would be addressed at the next meeting. “We have made fair demands. Thousands of nurses have joined the protest. We want the govt to resolve our grievances,” she told reporters after the meeting.Nurses began the strike near Rajarathinam Stadium in Egmore on Monday, seeking permanent employment, job security, and equal pay for equal work. They are also demanding a monthly salary of ₹45,000 and payment of pending incentives. They also sought medical and maternity leave, promotions, and higher incentives. “We are on contract, and we get about ₹21,000 a month, though our job profile is just like any other govt staff nurse. Many of us are posted in health and wellness centres. Our incentives for 2023 and 2024 are pending. We have also not received the promised 5% increment since 2023. articles.title: Talks could secure long-term future of Aberdeen Arts Centre
articles.summary: Castlegate Arts, which is holding discussions with city councillors, lost council funding last year.
articles.body:
The future of Aberdeen Arts Centre has been given a boost after councillors agreed to enter negotiations on a new long-term lease.

The charity which runs the venue, Castlegate Arts, has so far raised £350,000 towards a three-year £660,000 funding target, launched after it lost council funding last year.

City councillors have unanimously agreed to extend the lease on the arts centre beyond its expiry next January, and to begin talks on a new 30-year deal with an option to purchase.

A £50,000 grant is also to be provided for electrical upgrades.

More stories from North East Scotland, Orkney and Shetland

Listen to news from North East Scotland on BBC Sounds

Last year, Aberdeen City Council said the funding application submitted by the centre was not accepted as it did not meet its guidance for grant-giving.

The move prompted the launch of a major fundraising effort backed by the Aberdeen-born actress and Call the Midwife star Laura Main, who featured in many performances at the arts centre as a teenager.

Behind-the-scenes discussions among councillors have led to unanimous backing for a motion from independent councillor Marie Boulton.

The council has agreed to provide a grant for required electrical upgrades in the short term, while also agreeing to enter negotiations for a new lease of at least 30 years.

Castlegate Arts could later be given the option to purchase the building on King Street.

The council and Castlegate Arts will also collaborate on a new long-term funding and development model, which will allow it to apply for major capital grants.

A report on these discussions, with alternative options and a costed business case, is to be drawn up in time for next year's annual council budget.

Holly Paterson, executive director at Castlegate Arts, said: "We are pleased that Aberdeen City Council has today voted to work with us to secure the future of Aberdeen Arts Centre.

"We have built significant momentum over recent months, with incredible support from our communities, audiences, funders and partners.

"As the home of grassroots arts in Aberdeen, a hub for early-career creatives to develop and share new work, and a place for the community to come together, we are proud of what the arts centre provides for tens of thousands of people in the north east every year."

She said the centre was looking forward to working with councillors and officials to protect the community space.
